section.title: The Way of False Teachers
section.sectionRationale: Peter's exposure of the false teachers reaches full heat. He unmasks their arrogance and bestial appetites, links them to greedy Balaam, pictures them as empty springs promising a freedom they cannot give, and warns that their end, having known the way of righteousness and turned back, is worse than their beginning.
section.thesis: The false teachers are bold, greedy, and enslaved to corruption; like Balaam they love the wages of sin, and though they promise freedom they are slaves, so that having known the way of righteousness and turned from it, their last state is worse than the first.
section.frameNote: Four movements: their arrogance and bestial nature, verses 10 to 12; their debauchery and the way of Balaam, verses 13 to 16; empty springs and false freedom, verses 17 to 19; and the worse-than-before end of apostasy, verses 20 to 22.

verses.text: Such punishment is specially reserved for those who indulge the corrupt desires of the flesh and despise authority. Bold and {{authades|self-willed}}, they are unafraid to slander {{doxas|glorious beings}}.
Yet not even angels, though greater in strength and power, dare to bring such slanderous charges against them before the Lord.

These men are like {{aloga|irrational animals}}, creatures of instinct, born to be captured and destroyed. They blaspheme in matters they do not understand, and like such creatures, they too will be destroyed.

units.label: Debauchery and the way of Balaam

verses.text: The harm they will suffer is the wages of their wickedness. They consider it a pleasure to carouse in broad daylight. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deception as they feast with you.
Their eyes are full of adultery; their desire for sin is never satisfied; they seduce the unstable. They are accursed children with hearts trained in {{pleonexia|greed}}.
They have left the straight way and wandered off to follow the {{Balaam|way of Balaam}} son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness.
But he was rebuked for his transgression by a donkey, otherwise without speech, that spoke with a man’s voice and restrained the prophet’s madness.
These men are springs without water and mists driven by a storm. {{zophos|Blackest darkness}} is reserved for them.
With lofty but empty words, they appeal to the sensual passions of the flesh and entice those who are just escaping from others who live in error.
They promise them {{eleutheria|freedom}}, while they themselves are slaves to depravity. For a man is a slave to whatever has mastered him.

If indeed they have escaped the corruption of the world through the {{epignosis|knowledge}} of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, only to be entangled and overcome by it again, their final condition is worse than it was at first.
It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than to have known it and then to turn away from the holy commandment passed on to them.
Of them the proverbs are true: “A dog returns to its vomit,” and, “A sow that is washed goes back to her wallowing in the mud.”

authades.gloss: Self-willed, arrogant, stubbornly bent on one's own way. It describes a person who pleases himself and defies all authority. The false teachers are so self-willed that they do not fear even to slander beings the angels themselves treat with restraint.

doxas.gloss: Literally glories, here glorious ones or majestic beings, likely angelic powers. The false teachers rashly slander these, whereas even the mightier angels will not. It exposes their reckless arrogance in matters they do not understand.

aloga.gloss: Without reason, irrational, brute. Peter compares the false teachers to irrational animals of instinct. Governed by appetite rather than reason and truth, they are, like beasts, headed for capture and destruction.

pleonexia.gloss: Greed, covetousness, the restless craving for more. Their hearts are trained, literally exercised, in greed. Like athletes practiced in their sport, they are expert in coveting, a settled and disciplined habit of grasping.

Balaam.gloss: Balaam son of Beor, the prophet who loved reward and led Israel into sin, Numbers 22 to 24 and 31:16. He is the archetype of the teacher who trades his gift for money. The false teachers walk his way, prophesying for profit and enticing others into sin.

zophos.gloss: Gloom, deep darkness, the blackness of the nether world. Like waterless springs that promise refreshment and give none, the false teachers are destined for the blackest darkness, a fitting end for those who lead others astray.

eleutheria.gloss: Freedom, liberty. The false teachers promise freedom, twisting grace into a license to sin. Yet they are themselves slaves to depravity, offering a counterfeit liberty that is really bondage. True freedom is found only in submission to Christ.

epignosis.gloss: Full, personal knowledge, here of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. These teachers had come to a real acquaintance with the gospel and outwardly escaped the world's corruption, yet turned back. Their knowledge was informed but not saving, making their fall all the more grievous.

basic.context: Peter now paints the false teachers in full color. They are arrogant and driven by lust, so bold they slander beings even angels treat carefully. They are like brute animals ruled by instinct, greedy, adulterous, and seductive. Like Balaam, the prophet who took money to harm God's people, they trade truth for gain. They are empty, springs with no water, promising freedom while they are slaves to their own sin. Worst of all, they had known the way of Christ and turned back, so their end is worse than their beginning, like a dog returning to its vomit.
basic.hermeneutics: This section is vivid, poetic denunciation, closely parallel to Jude. Two points draw debate. First, the slander of glorious beings, verses 10 to 11: what are these beings, and what is the restraint even angels show? Second, and more weighty, verses 20 to 22: had these teachers been truly saved and then lost, or did they only outwardly reform and never truly belong to Christ? The passage warns urgently against turning back, whichever view one holds.
basic.originalLanguages: The teachers are authades, self-willed, so arrogant they slander the doxas, the glorious ones. They are like aloga, irrational animals, with hearts trained in pleonexia, greed, walking the way of Balaam. They are waterless springs bound for zophos, blackest darkness, promising eleutheria, freedom, while enslaved. Having known Christ by epignosis and turned back, their last state is worse than the first.
basic.typology: Balaam is a type of the false teacher: the gifted prophet who loved money and led God's people into sin. His talking donkey, more perceptive than the prophet, exposes the madness of prophesying for profit. The proverbs of the dog and the sow picture the apostate's return to filth, a warning against treating cleansing lightly.
basic.christ: The tragedy of these teachers is measured by Christ: they had come to know our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and escaped the world's corruption through Him, yet turned away. Christ is the way of righteousness they abandoned and the only Master whose service is true freedom. Their false liberty is exposed against His real deliverance from sin's slavery.
basic.god: God is the righteous Judge who has reserved blackest darkness for those who corrupt His people, and He is holy, so that turning from the way of righteousness is grave beyond words. He is also the giver of true freedom, whose commandment is holy and whose way leads to life, against every counterfeit the false teachers peddle.
basic.crossReferences: Jude 1:10-13 and 16 give the parallel denunciation, including Balaam and the images of waterless clouds. Numbers 22 to 24 and 31:16 tell of Balaam. Proverbs 26:11 is the dog and its vomit. And Matthew 12:43-45 describes the last state worse than the first.
basic.oneStory: The way of Balaam, greed dressed as prophecy, runs through every age of God's people. Peter sets the false teachers on that ancient road and warns of its end in darkness. Against their empty, enslaving promises stands Christ, the way of righteousness and the giver of true freedom, whose people are called never to return to the mire from which He washed them.

context.literary:
The paragraph is a portrait gallery. Where verses 4 to 9 argued from history, verses 10 to 22 describe, and the description moves in three waves. The first, verses 10 to 13, is about contempt and appetite: despising authority, speaking evil of what they do not understand, and then living like animals. The second, verses 14 to 16, turns from the group to the person of Balaam, one example set against the whole company. The third, verses 17 to 22, moves to the damage these men do to others and finally to themselves, and it ends with two proverbs that stop the argument cold.

The structure has a quiet symmetry. The section begins with judgment already 'reserved' in verse 10 and ends with a 'blackest darkness' reserved in verse 17, and then a final condition that is 'worse than at first' in verse 20. Peter keeps returning to the idea of a verdict that was set before the teachers began. The word 'reserved' is the same verb that held the angels in verse 4 and the heavens for fire in 3:7.

There is a chain of images, and each one fails the same way. Animals are creatures of instinct born to be caught. Springs promise water and give none. Mists driven by a storm look like rain and blow past. Words are 'lofty but empty'. The teachers appear to offer what a thirsty person wants and deliver nothing, and the images are chosen to expose a gap between appearance and substance.

The paragraph also has an inside and an outside. Verses 10 to 16 describe what the false teachers are in themselves. Verses 17 to 22 describe what they do to the unstable, and the point where the two meet is verse 19: they promise freedom and are themselves slaves. The last two verses, with their 'known the way... turn away', are written to make a reader stop and look at himself, and the choice of proverbs, one from Scripture and one from common speech, closes the chapter by dropping the argument into the plain language of the street.
context.historical:
The picture of Balaam would have been familiar to every Jewish reader. In Numbers 22 to 24 Balak king of Moab sends elders 'with the fees for divination in hand' to hire the prophet, Numbers 22:7. Balaam repeatedly says he can speak only what the LORD puts in his mouth, Numbers 23:12, and even wishes to die 'the death of the righteous', Numbers 23:10. Yet Numbers 31:16 tells that it was through his counsel that Israel was drawn into the sin at Peor, Numbers 25:1 to 3, where idol feasts and immorality brought a plague. Deuteronomy 23:4 and 5 and Nehemiah 13:2 remember him as the man hired to curse God's people, and Micah 6:5 tells Israel to remember what he said. In Revelation 2:14 'the teaching of Balaam' is one that leads to food offered to idols and sexual immorality. By Peter's day his name had become a byword for a gifted man who sold his gift.

The feasts of verse 13 belong to the early church's meals together. Paul in 1 Corinthians 11:20 to 22 rebukes the church for turning the Lord's Supper into a place where one goes hungry and another gets drunk, and Jude 12 calls the false teachers 'hidden reefs in your love feasts'. A few early manuscripts of 2 Peter read 'love feasts' in place of 'deceptions' in verse 13, which shows how readily the two letters were read together. To carouse in daylight was a mark of shame in the ancient world: in Acts 2:15 Peter himself can say the disciples cannot be drunk because it is only the third hour of the day, and Paul says that drunkards get drunk at night, 1 Thessalonians 5:7.

The talk of freedom has a setting. Corinth had a slogan, 'All things are lawful for me', 1 Corinthians 6:12, and Paul has to answer in Galatians 5:13 that freedom is not an opportunity for the flesh. Teachers who promised liberty from moral rules would find an audience among new believers who had only recently left pagan households, the 'just escaping' of verse 18. The dog and the pig were both unclean animals to a Jew, Leviticus 11:7, and 'dog' was a term of contempt, Philippians 3:2.
context.canonical:
The story of Balaam reaches across the Bible. After the Moabite king hires him in Numbers 22 to 24, the narrative of Numbers 25 and 31 shows the real damage done by his counsel, and Deuteronomy 23:4 and 5 and Nehemiah 13:2 repeat that God turned the curse into blessing. Jude 11 says the false teachers 'rushed headlong into the error of Balaam', and Revelation 2:14 shows the same teaching at work in the church at Pergamum. His whole history is a lesson in how a true word and a false heart can sit together. The irony that so unsettles readers is that the same man gave a true oracle of the star from Jacob in Numbers 24:17, and Peter has just referred to a morning star in 1:19.

The image of the dry spring comes from the prophets. 'They have forsaken Me, the fountain of living water, and they have dug their own cisterns', Jeremiah 2:13, and Jeremiah can complain to God that He has become to him 'like a mirage... water that is not there', Jeremiah 15:18. Job 6:15 speaks of faithless wadis. The claim to freedom that ends in slavery is taken up by Jesus, 'everyone who sins is a slave to sin', John 8:34, by Paul, Romans 6:16, and by Peter's own first letter, 1 Peter 2:16.

The warning about the last state being worse than the first comes from Jesus, who uses it of the house swept clean in Matthew 12:43 to 45 and Luke 11:24 to 26, and whom Peter echoes nearly word for word. The proverb of the dog comes from Proverbs 26:11. Hebrews 6:4 to 6 and 10:26 to 29 deal with the same hard subject from another side, and 1 John 2:19 offers a counterweight, 'They went out from us, but they did not belong to us.' Peter's own conclusion in 3:17 and 18, a call to be on guard and grow, shows the pastoral purpose of all these warnings.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Peter paints these men in such strong colors because his readers are in danger of finding them attractive. The teachers are bold, fluent and promise liberty. A frank picture of their lives, their greed and their end is the antidote. He wants the believers to look past the words to the way of life and to see that a message of freedom delivered by someone who is himself unfree should not be believed.

He also wants the church to stay clear about authority. These men despise it and slander what they do not understand, and Peter sets before them the angels' restraint in verse 11 as a sober contrast. Humility before God, and before the delegated authorities He has set, is the mark of the true servant, and bluster is the mark of the false.

The last verses are meant to protect the unstable, whom the teachers target in verse 14. Peter does not leave the readers with a mere condemnation. He has told them what these men promise, how they appeal, and what they do. The aim is that those 'just escaping' will not be pulled back, and that those who have escaped will count the knowledge of Christ as more than a phase. The warning is severe because the thing at stake is not a lapse but a return.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage is mostly description. It reports what the false teachers do and what will happen to them, and it does not instruct believers to treat anyone who falls into sin as a dog or a pig. The proverbs describe the settled character of the men in question, not every Christian who stumbles. Peter himself denied Jesus and was restored, John 21:15 to 19, and no reader should use verses 20 to 22 to write off a believer who is struggling and repenting.

The prescriptive force comes by implication. Do not follow these teachers, do not be seduced by their promises of freedom, and do not turn from the holy commandment once received. In 3:17 and 18 Peter makes the commands explicit, to be on guard and to grow.

The account of Balaam and his donkey should be read as a record, not a template. Peter does not tell us to look for speaking animals, only to see that God can restrain a prophet's madness by humbling means. Likewise the 'slandering of glorious beings' is described as a fault of arrogance, and no instruction is given here about how believers ought to speak of angelic or demonic powers beyond the restraint that Jude 9 illustrates.

debates.question: Who are the 'glorious beings' these teachers slander, verses 10 and 11?

views.label: Angelic powers, good or fallen
views.case: The word is 'glories', and most readers take it for angelic majesties. Jude 8 to 10 sets the same charge beside the archangel Michael, who would not bring a slanderous charge even against the devil but said, 'The Lord rebuke you!' On this reading the teachers boast of authority over the unseen realm while even the angels show restraint before the Lord.

views.label: Fallen angels and demons in particular
views.case: Others notice that Michael's restraint was toward the devil, and argue that the teachers mock demonic powers with a swagger that ignores how dangerous they are. The principle is that no creature should handle spiritual powers lightly.

views.label: Human rulers and church leaders
views.case: A minority take the glories as human dignitaries, in keeping with the phrase 'despise authority' in verse 10. The angels' contrast would then be that even beings of greater power do not abuse the authority of others.

debates.bearing: The comparison with angels in verse 11 is the strongest guide, and most readers take it for spiritual beings. Whichever view is taken, Peter's concern is not the technical identification but the proud tongue, which he sets over against the humility of heaven itself.

debates.question: Were these teachers once truly saved, verses 20 to 22?

views.label: They were genuine believers who fell away
views.case: The language of escaping the corruption of the world through knowing 'our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ' sounds like the language of conversion, as in 1:4. On this reading a person can know Christ and be lost, and the severity of verse 21 fits those who had truly received light.

views.label: They had outward reform but never real new birth
views.case: Others point out that Peter writes 'if indeed' and never says they were born again. Jesus warned that many who say 'Lord, Lord' will hear 'I never knew you', Matthew 7:21 to 23, and the dog and the sow return to what they were because their nature was never changed. 1 John 2:19 says of those who left, 'they did not belong to us.' Knowledge of the way is not the same as a new heart.

views.label: A warning that works through the believer
views.case: A third view treats the passage as a means God uses to keep His people: the warning is real and the danger is real, and those who heed it are the ones who persevere, as Philippians 1:6 and 1 Peter 1:5 promise. Peter's own aim, 3:17 and 18, is to keep the readers from falling, and the severity serves that end.

debates.bearing: All three agree on what Peter wants: that no one treat knowing about Christ as a guarantee, and that no one drift back toward the old ways. The passage is a serious warning, and its seriousness does not need to be softened or sharpened to be heard.

study.originalLanguages:
The language in this paragraph is vivid, and several of its words are worth slowing down for. The first adjective in verse 10 describes the teachers as bold, tolmetes, a word for a daring person; 'bold and self-willed' is a pair in which the first word names the nerve and the second the stubbornness. They 'blaspheme', blasphemeo, in matters they do not understand, which is the verb used of insulting God and of abusing people, and it appears in verses 10 and 12 and again in verse 2 where the way of truth is 'defamed'. Peter's repetition shows that their speech is the main weapon.

In verse 13 the 'pleasure' they take in daytime carousing is hedone, from which comes our word hedonism, and the 'carousing' is tryphe, a word for soft, extravagant living. They are called 'blots and blemishes', spiloi and momoi. The second word is the one used for the flaw that disqualified a sacrificial animal, and in 3:14 Peter says the believers should be found 'spotless and blameless', aspiloi and amometoi. The two lists are opposite in every letter. Jude 12 speaks of 'hidden reefs in your love feasts', and a few manuscripts of 2 Peter read 'love feasts' instead of 'deceptions' in verse 13, which shows how the two texts were read together.

Verse 14 says their eyes are 'full of adultery', literally full of an adulteress, and that they 'seduce' the unstable. The verb for seduce comes from the word for bait on a hook, and it is the same verb James 1:14 uses of a person being 'enticed' by his own desire. Peter uses it again in verse 18. The teachers fish for the unsettled and the new. Their hearts are 'trained' in greed, gymnazo, the language of the gymnasium. Greed is a discipline that they have practised until it is second nature. They are 'accursed children', a Semitic way of saying people marked for a curse, set against the 'children' of promise.

In verse 15 the BSB has 'Balaam son of Beor'. Some Greek manuscripts read Bosor, most likely a Semitic shaping of the same name. The phrase 'wages of wickedness' is misthos adikias, and the same phrase in Acts 1:18 names what Judas received for his betrayal, so the combination of a prophet's office with a payment for evil appears in both stories. The donkey 'restrained' the prophet's paraphronia, which means a being beside one's mind, madness, and Peter's wry point is that a dumb animal showed more sense than the seer.

In verse 18, 'lofty but empty words' is huperonka mataiotetos, bombast, swollen words of emptiness. Mataiotes is the same word for 'futility' in Romans 8:20 and Ephesians 4:17, where it describes a world and a mind under sin. The teachers produce the very futility they claim to free people from.

Verse 19 has a hinge in two forms of one verb. The teachers are 'slaves of corruption' and 'whatever has mastered him' translates a verb meaning to be overcome, hettaomai, which returns in verse 20 where they are 'overcome' again after being entangled. Peter says that whatever has overcome a person has also enslaved him. The word for 'corruption', phthora, links to 1:4, where believers have escaped it, and to 2:12, where the teachers are destroyed in their own corruption, so that the whole chapter frames escape and return.

In verse 21 the 'holy commandment passed on' uses paradidomi, to hand over, the vocabulary of tradition, as in Jude 3 where the faith was 'entrusted once for all'. 'The way of righteousness' has roots in the Old Testament idea of the two ways and in the Gospels' account of John coming 'in a righteous way', Matthew 21:32. The first-century church was itself called the Way in Acts 9:2.

typology.type: Balaam the hired prophet, verses 15 and 16
typology.fulfillment: Balak sends elders with the fees for divination, Numbers 22:7, and Balaam, though he speaks God's words, loves the reward and finally leads Israel into sin at Peor, Numbers 31:16. He is a standing pattern of the gifted man whose ministry is for sale. Jude 11 and Revelation 2:14 take the pattern and apply it to later teachers. The escalation lies in the true Prophet, who refused every kingdom of the world offered for worship, Matthew 4:8 to 10, and who gave His life for His flock, John 10:11. The type falls short because Balaam did speak a true oracle, Numbers 24:17, while the false teachers have none.

typology.type: The donkey that saw the angel, verse 16
typology.fulfillment: The animal sees the angel of the LORD with the drawn sword when the prophet does not, Numbers 22:23, and speaks when the LORD opens her mouth, 22:28. The correspondence is that God sometimes shows humbling truth through the lowliest messenger, so that human pride is silenced by what it despises. The escalation is in Christ, who rode a donkey into Jerusalem, Matthew 21:5, and who is the Word that does not merely rebuke a prophet but speaks life. The type falls short because the donkey's speech was a single act of rescue, while Christ's speech is God's final word, Hebrews 1:2.

In dry country a spring that fails is a bitter betrayal, and Jeremiah 2:13 sets the failed cisterns of idolatry against the LORD, the 'fountain of living water'. Jesus takes up the image and says that anyone who drinks the water He gives will never thirst, John 4:13 and 14, and in John 7:37 He invites the thirsty to come to Him and drink. The escalation is from a prophet's complaint to a Person who fulfils the promise. The type falls short in that a failing spring is only a disappointment, while the Son's offer, once refused, leaves a person with nothing else, as verse 17 says.

typology.type: The dog and the washed sow, verse 22
typology.fulfillment: The two animals were unclean to a Jew, Leviticus 11:7, and the dog's return to its vomit is Proverbs 26:11. They stand as a picture of cleansing that touches the outside and leaves the nature unchanged. The contrast is with the new birth, in which Christ gives a new heart, Ezekiel 36:25 to 27, and Paul can say believers 'were washed', 1 Corinthians 6:11. The escalation is from outward washing to inner renewal by the Spirit. The pattern falls short because proverbs describe a tendency in animals, while Scripture speaks of the possibility of a changed nature.

study.christ:
The pivotal phrase in this paragraph is in verse 20: 'our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ', the full title Peter has used since the first verse of the letter, 1:1 and 1:11, and the one he will use again in 3:18. Knowing Him is the thing that rescues a person from the world's corruption. The terrible fact about the false teachers is not simply that they are wicked but that they have stood close to the light, and Peter measures their ruin by what Christ offers.

Christ is also the true freedom. The teachers promise liberty and give slavery, and Jesus says, 'If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed', John 8:36, and 'It is for freedom that Christ has set us free', Galatians 5:1. His freedom is not licence to follow appetites but release from them, so that Paul can say believers have 'become slaves to righteousness', Romans 6:18. Against every counterfeit liberty stands the One whose service is the only way to be free.

The way of righteousness is a way that Christ walked and is. Peter calls the gospel a 'holy commandment' and a way, and the same way is the one Jesus names Himself in John 14:6. To turn from it is to turn from a person, and Hebrews 10:29 shows how grave that is: to trample the Son of God and insult the Spirit of grace.

There is also a contrast in the Christ who restrains Himself. Verse 11 says that even angels do not bring slanderous charges before the Lord, and 1 Peter 2:23 says of Jesus that when He was reviled He did not revile in return. The humility of heaven is seen in its fullest form in the Son who bore insult without answering. The false teachers speak evil of what they do not understand, and the Lord whom they deny took evil upon Himself.

We should avoid forcing the animals into allegory. The dog and the sow are not types of Christ in any sense, and the donkey is not Christ. The use of the donkey in the Gospels at Palm Sunday is a different matter. What the passage gives is a negative portrait that is measured against Christ: He is what these men are not, and what they have abandoned is the fullness of life in Him.
study.god:
God appears in this paragraph as the Lord who judges contempt. Peter says that punishment is 'specially reserved' for those who despise authority and indulge the flesh, and that blackest darkness is reserved for the false teachers. God is not careless about how people speak of Him and of His servants, and the angels, who stand nearest to Him, know it. Their restraint in verse 11 is not weakness, it is reverence: even they do not take judgment out of the Lord's hands.

He is also a God who has authority over language. He gives a donkey a man's voice and restrains the prophet's madness. Nothing in the account of Balaam is outside His control: the hired prophet cannot curse, and the curse turns to blessing, Deuteronomy 23:5. The same God who turns curses into blessings does not allow His church to be handed to a hired voice.

The passage shows God as holy. The commandment is 'holy', the way is the way of 'righteousness', and the stain on the teachers is a stain on what is clean. The believers are to be 'spotless and blameless', 3:14, and the language of the sanctuary hovers over the whole paragraph. A holy God does not treat the entrance of corruption into His people as a small matter.

He is a God of true freedom. The teachers misuse the word, but Peter does not give it up; there is a freedom to be had, and it is a freedom from mastery by sin. God's commandments are not chains, and obedience is the shape of a liberated life.

There is a tension that the passage holds. God's judgment is certain and the way back is not easy, yet verses 20 to 22 are given as warnings in a letter that is full of promises, 1:3 and 4. The God of the passage does not delight in judging; He warns precisely because He is merciful. Ezekiel 18:23 asks, 'Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked?', and the very severity of Peter's words belongs to that mercy.

For worship, the passage teaches fear in the right measure. To know the Lord and Savior is to be near a holy God, and nearness calls for care. We hold fast, not because we trust our own grip, but because we have seen what happens to those who treat the holy commandment as cheap.

crossReferences.note: Jude's list of images, irrational animals, hidden reefs, waterless clouds, fruitless trees, wild waves and wandering stars, runs alongside Peter's. Jude names Cain, Balaam and Korah; Peter picks out Balaam, so the two letters complement each other on the same men.

The story of the donkey and the angel with the drawn sword. The animal sees what the prophet does not, and the LORD opens her mouth. Peter's 'rebuked for his transgression by a donkey' is a summary of this scene, and the angel's words 'your way is perverse before me' in verse 32 name the sin directly.

Moses says the women of Moab caused Israel to turn unfaithfully through the counsel of Balaam at Peor. This is how a prophet who spoke God's words became a cause of Israel's ruin, and why Peter says Balaam loved the wages of wickedness.

Balaam says he cannot curse what God has not cursed and will speak only what the LORD puts in his mouth, and he wishes to die the death of the righteous. These words make him a puzzle, a man who spoke truth and chose gain, and make the pattern of Peter's teachers harder to dismiss.

Jesus tells the church at Pergamum that some hold 'the teaching of Balaam', who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before Israel through food offered to idols and sexual immorality. The same pattern persists in the early church, and shows that Balaam's name stood for a type of teaching.

A dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly. Peter's first proverb is taken straight from here. The Old Testament text speaks of folly, and Peter applies it to those who turn back from truth once known.

Jesus tells of the unclean spirit that returns to the house swept clean and brings seven others, so that the final plight is worse than the first. Peter's 'worse than it was at first' echoes the saying, and the passage shows that cleaning without filling leaves a person open.

God accuses His people of forsaking the fountain of living water for broken cisterns that cannot hold water. The false teachers' springs without water are the same failure, a promise of refreshment that cannot be kept.

Jesus says everyone who sins is a slave to sin. This is the principle behind Peter's verse 19, that a person is a slave to whatever has mastered him, and it shows Peter was repeating what the Lord had taught.

Paul says that people are slaves to whom they obey, whether to sin leading to death or to obedience leading to righteousness. It sets verse 19 in the structure of the gospel: there is no neutral freedom, only a choice of masters, and Christ is the one master whose service is freedom.

The writer warns that deliberately going on sinning after receiving the knowledge of the truth leaves no sacrifice, and that one who tramples the Son of God deserves greater punishment. It runs parallel to 2 Peter 2:20 to 22 and shows the same weight on knowing and then turning.

John says those who left the fellowship never belonged to it, for if they had they would have stayed. It stands as a counterweight to the reading that these teachers had been true believers, and it shows how the early church understood apostasy.

study.oneStory:
The paragraph answers a question that begins in Eden: what happens when the creature takes what the Creator has given and uses it for himself? The serpent promised freedom and delivered slavery, and Genesis 3 shows the pattern that Peter now describes in these teachers. Their promise is the promise of the garden, that you will be like God, and the end is the same, nakedness and exile.

Balaam brings the story into Israel's own history. He stands at the border of the land and sees Israel through a prophet's eyes, and yet he sells his gift. His counsel at Peor is a second fall, Israel drawn into idolatry and immorality at the threshold of the land, Numbers 25. The false teachers of Peter's day are a third. Every generation has its Balaam, and Revelation 2:14 shows he does not stop with the apostles.

The image of freedom and slavery runs through the whole Bible. Israel was a slave in Egypt and was set free to serve the LORD, Exodus 4:23. The prophets show them returning to slavery by idolatry. In Christ the true liberation comes, 'if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed', and the church lives in the tension between the freedom won and the old ways that try to bring it back. Peter writes in that tension, to a church that has escaped Egypt and is tempted to look back.

The passage looks forward to the day when the warnings will end. Jesus says the weeds and the wheat grow together until the harvest, Matthew 13:30, and in the new creation there is nothing that defiles, Revelation 21:27. The false teachers, the dog and the sow, are outside the city, Revelation 22:15. But within the new creation those who held fast are given the morning star, Revelation 2:28, and the waterless springs are replaced by 'the river of the water of life', Revelation 22:1. What the false teachers promised and could not give is given freely by the Lamb.

The paragraph therefore belongs in the story as a warning against a repeated mistake. The first human beings believed that freedom lay in setting aside God's word. The last book of the Bible shows where that road ends, and the whole story between them invites people to take the other road, the way of righteousness, in company with the Lord and Savior who walked it first.

sermon.title: “False Teachers among You”, Part Two
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in 2 Peter, this message treats 2 Peter 2:10-22 directly, the arrogance and greed of the false teachers, the way of Balaam, their false promise of freedom, and the solemn warning of turning back. A clear, orthodox handling of this movement.

quiz.q: How does Peter expose the arrogance of the false teachers in verses 10 to 12?

options.text: They are self-willed and so bold they slander glorious beings that even angels treat with restraint.
options.note: Verses 10 to 11: their reckless contempt outstrips even the mightier angels' caution.

options.text: They are humble teachers who simply made honest mistakes.
options.note: Peter portrays proud, brute-like arrogance, not honest error.

options.text: They behave like irrational animals ruled by instinct.
options.note: True to verse 12, though the arrogance is seen most in their slander of glorious beings.

options.text: They are overly cautious and fearful in spiritual matters.
options.note: The opposite: they are unafraid where even angels show restraint.

quiz.q: Why does Peter compare the false teachers to Balaam?

options.text: Because, like Balaam, they love the wages of wickedness and trade their teaching for gain.
options.note: Verse 15: Balaam is the archetype of the prophet who serves money and leads others to sin.

options.text: Because they, like Balaam, were faithful prophets of God.
options.note: Balaam is a warning, not a model of faithfulness.

options.text: Because they have wandered from the straight way for profit.
options.note: True to verse 15, though the heart of the comparison is Balaam's love of reward.

options.text: Because they were rebuked by talking animals.
options.note: The donkey rebuked Balaam; the point is his greed, not a shared experience.

quiz.q: What is ironic about the freedom the false teachers promise?

options.text: They promise freedom while they themselves are slaves to depravity.
options.note: Verse 19: a man is a slave to whatever has mastered him; their liberty is counterfeit.

options.text: They deliver a genuine and lasting freedom.
options.note: Their freedom is a counterfeit; they are enslaved to sin.

options.text: They offer a liberty that is really bondage to sin.
options.note: True, that is the irony, rooted in their own slavery.

options.text: They promise freedom only to those already mature in faith.
options.note: They target the unstable and those just escaping error, not the mature.

quiz.q: What makes the end of these teachers worse than their beginning?

options.text: They had come to know the way of righteousness in Christ and then turned away from it.
options.note: Verses 20 to 21: to know the holy commandment and forsake it is graver than never knowing it.

options.text: They simply never heard the gospel at all.
options.note: The tragedy is precisely that they had known it and turned back.

options.text: They became entangled again in the corruption they had escaped.
options.note: True to verse 20, though the depth is that they knew Christ and abandoned Him.

options.text: They suffered worse poverty than before.
options.note: The worse condition is spiritual and eternal, not material.

quiz.q: What do the proverbs of the dog and the sow illustrate in verse 22?

options.text: The apostate returns to the filth he seemed to leave, an outward cleansing without a changed heart.
options.note: Verse 22: the animals return to their nature, picturing turning back to sin.

options.text: That true believers can never fall in any sense.
options.note: The proverbs illustrate the warning of turning back, a point debated but not dismissed.

options.text: That God delights to wash and restore the repentant.
options.note: Here the images depict return to filth, not restoration.

options.text: That people tend to revert to their unchanged nature.
options.note: True to the images, though Peter applies it pointedly to those who forsake the way.

questions: The false teachers offered freedom but delivered slavery. Where have you been tempted to mistake license for true freedom, and what does real freedom in Christ look like?
Balaam loved the wages of wickedness. In what subtle ways can the love of money or reward pull a heart away from faithfulness to God?
Peter warns of knowing the way of righteousness and turning back. What helps you keep pressing forward rather than drifting toward what Christ has rescued you from?
The teachers targeted the unstable and those just escaping error. How can your church better protect and ground new or struggling believers?
A washed sow returns to the mud when its nature is unchanged. How does the reality of a truly changed heart in Christ give you hope against falling back?

translationNotes.note: Glorious beings renders doxas, literally glories; a footnote allows to blaspheme angelic majesties, most likely spiritual or angelic powers.
Hearts trained in greed uses an athletic term, exercised or practiced, picturing a disciplined habit of coveting.
A footnote notes manuscripts reading Bosor for Beor; Balaam son of Beor is the prophet of Numbers 22 to 24.
The first proverb quotes Proverbs 26:11; the second, the washed sow, is a common proverbial saying, both picturing a return to filth.
